extraction.comparison_type: Increasing dietary vitamin A intake (dose-response, per unit increase)
extraction.timing: retrospective exposure assessment by questionnaire after hospital admission
extraction.location: First Affiliated Hospital of West China University of Medical Sciences
extraction.population: Hospitalized men with prostate cancer matched to other malignant tumor cases and other urological (non-malignant) cases

sample_size.excerpt: Twenty-seven cases of prostate cancer were matched with an equal number of other malignant tumor cases (non-urological tumor) and other urological cases (non-malignant tumor).

cases.excerpt: Twenty-seven cases of prostate cancer were matched with an equal number of other malignant tumor cases (non-urological tumor) and other urological cases (non-malignant tumor).

effect_size.excerpt: Increasing dietary vitamin A was associated with a significant decrease in the risk of prostate cancer (RR = 0.948, 95% CI = 0.9309-0.9947, P = 0.029).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Increasing dietary vitamin A was associated with a significant decrease in the risk of prostate cancer (RR = 0.948, 95% CI = 0.9309-0.9947, P = 0.029).

comparison.excerpt: This factor also showed dose response gradients. The relative risk was decreasing with exposure dose increasing.

design.excerpt: A 1:2 matched case-control study was used to determine the risk factors of prostate cancer.

timing.excerpt: The questionnaire was used to survey the both groups of patients.

location.excerpt: All of these patients were treated in the First Affiliated Hospital of West China University of Medical Sciences.

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Such data as diet, lifestyle, marital status and past history of other prostate diseases were obtained.

sample_size.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

cases.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Fat from dairy products (with the exception of butter) or fish was unrelated to risk. Saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, and alpha-linolenic acid, but not linoleic acid, were associated with advanced prostate cancer risk; only the association with alpha-linolenic acid persisted when saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, linoleic acid, and alpha-linolenic acid were modeled simultaneously (multivariate RR = 3.43; 95% CI = 1.67-7.04; P [trend] = .002).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, and alpha-linolenic acid, but not linoleic acid, were associated with advanced prostate cancer risk; only the association with alpha-linolenic acid persisted when saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, linoleic acid, and alpha-linolenic acid were modeled simultaneously (multivariate RR = 3.43; 95% CI = 1.67-7.04; P [trend] = .002).

validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort reports the omega-3 fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid in relation to incident advanced prostate cancer, though the abstract does not report total or marine omega-3 intake separately.

extraction.comparison_type: high versus low quintile of intake, multivariate model (alpha-linolenic acid)
extraction.timing: prospective, exposure assessed in 1986 before prostate cancer diagnosis
extraction.population: U.S. male health professionals aged 40 through 75 in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study

sample_size.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

cases.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Fat from dairy products (with the exception of butter) or fish was unrelated to risk. Saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, and alpha-linolenic acid, but not linoleic acid, were associated with advanced prostate cancer risk; only the association with alpha-linolenic acid persisted when saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, linoleic acid, and alpha-linolenic acid were modeled simultaneously (multivariate RR = 3.43; 95% CI = 1.67-7.04; P [trend] = .002).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, and alpha-linolenic acid, but not linoleic acid, were associated with advanced prostate cancer risk; only the association with alpha-linolenic acid persisted when saturated fat, monounsaturated fat, linoleic acid, and alpha-linolenic acid were modeled simultaneously (multivariate RR = 3.43; 95% CI = 1.67-7.04; P [trend] = .002).

validated_results.title: A prospective study of dietary fat and risk of prostate cancer.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort reports a red meat-specific relative risk for incident advanced prostate cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: high versus low quintile of intake (food group with strongest positive association with advanced cancer)
extraction.timing: prospective, exposure assessed in 1986 before prostate cancer diagnosis
extraction.population: U.S. male health professionals aged 40 through 75 in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study

sample_size.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

cases.excerpt: As of January 31, 1990, 300 new cases of prostate cancer, including 126 advanced cases, were documented in 47855 participants initially free of diagnosed cancer.

effect_size.excerpt: Red meat represented the food group with the strongest positive association with advanced cancer (RR = 2.64; 95% CI = 1.21-5.77; P = .02). Fat from dairy products (with the exception of butter) or fish was unrelated to risk.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Red meat represented the food group with the strongest positive association with advanced cancer (RR = 2.64; 95% CI = 1.21-5.77; P = .02).
